auraIntro: Welcome home, Explorer. Review the classified briefing on our home galaxy, the Milky Way.
overview: The Milky Way is a barred spiral galaxy containing our Solar System, along with an estimated 100 to 400 billion stars.
formation: Formed approximately 13.6 billion years ago shortly after the Big Bang.
structure: Barred spiral with two major spiral arms (Scutum-Centaurus and Perseus) and central supermassive black hole Sagittarius A*.
discoveryHistory: Observed since antiquity as a band of light across the night sky. Galileo resolved it into individual stars in 1610.
observationTips: Best viewed on clear, moonless summer nights far from urban light pollution.
funFacts: Our Solar System orbits the galactic center at 828,000 km/h, taking ~240 million years per cosmic orbit.
The Milky Way and Andromeda are approaching each other at 110 km/s and will merge in ~4.5 billion years.

cards.title: Arrival: Our Cosmic Island
cards.subtitle: Barred Spiral Architecture
cards.body: Welcome to the Milky Way, a vast barred spiral galaxy spanning 100,000 light-years across deep space. Home to our Sun and between 100 and 400 billion other stars, its luminous disk is shaped by gravity into two primary spiral arms anchored by a central stellar bar.

cards.title: Discovery: Mapping From Within
cards.subtitle: How Humanity Unlocked Our Home Galaxy
cards.body: For millennia, humans viewed the Milky Way as a ghostly river of light. In 1610, Galileo Galilei aimed his telescope at the band and discovered it was composed of countless individual stars. In the 1920s, Harlow Shapley and Edwin Hubble proved that our Solar System sits in the disk far from the center, revealing our true cosmic address.
bulletPoints: Galileo first proved in 1610 that the milky band consists of faint star clusters.
Harlow Shapley mapped globular clusters to pinpoint the galactic center in Sagittarius.
Edwin Hubble proved spiral nebulae were external galaxies, establishing the scale of the universe.

cards.title: Cosmic Story: The Gravitational Core
cards.subtitle: Sagittarius A* and the Orion Spur
cards.body: At the exact gravitational core of the Milky Way lies Sagittarius A*, a supermassive black hole containing 4.1 million solar masses. Our Solar System orbits this central engine from a distance of 27,000 light-years inside the Orion Spur, traveling at 828,000 km/h to complete one cosmic orbit every 240 million years.
bulletPoints: Sagittarius A* exerts gravitational dominance over the inner stellar bulge.
Our Sun is located in the Orion Spur between the Sagittarius and Perseus arms.
Over 150 ancient globular star clusters orbit in the surrounding galactic halo.

cards.title: Deep Insight: Fermi Bubbles & Gaia Survey
cards.subtitle: High-Energy Mysteries Above the Disk
cards.body: Space telescopes have unveiled structures invisible to optical light. NASA's Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope discovered two giant Fermi Bubbles extending 25,000 light-years above and below the galactic plane—remnants of a colossal energetic eruption from Sgr A* millions of years ago. ESA's Gaia mission has mapped 1.8 billion stars in precision 3D.
bulletPoints: Fermi Bubbles emit high-energy gamma rays perpendicular to the galactic disk.
Gaia satellite precise astrometry maps stellar motion and galactic cannibalism history.
Ancient mergers like Gaia-Enceladus helped build the thick disk of our galaxy.

cards.title: Cosmic Curiosity: The Upcoming Collision
cards.subtitle: Milkomeda: Our Galactic Destiny
cards.body: The Milky Way is not stationary. It is traveling through the Local Group at high velocity, currently consuming small dwarf satellite galaxies like the Sagittarius Dwarf. In approximately 4.5 billion years, our galaxy will collide head-on with the giant Andromeda Galaxy, merging to form a giant elliptical galaxy dubbed 'Milkomeda'.
bulletPoints: Milky Way and Andromeda are approaching each other at 110 kilometers per second.
Stellar distances are so vast that individual stars will rarely collide during the merger.
Our Sun will be flung into a new orbit in the combined giant elliptical galaxy.
